blocks.text: In the 1966 Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, Surveyor-General Russell Gladstone Dick described electronic computers being used for the most demanding mathematical work in surveying and mapping. In the same account he called the office staff who performed calculations “computers” too—a useful reminder that a computer in a 1960s survey office could be a person or a machine.
blocks.markdown: In the 1966 Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, Surveyor-General Russell Gladstone Dick described electronic computers being used for the most demanding mathematical work in surveying and mapping. In the same account he called the office staff who performed calculations “computers” too—a useful reminder that a computer in a 1960s survey office could be a person or a machine.

sources.label: Russell Gladstone Dick, “Maps and mapping” (1966), Te Ara

blocks.text: The distinction matters when reading a claim that mapping had been computerised. A survey office could calculate coordinates electronically while draughting, photographic reproduction and final map compilation still happened through established production methods.

blocks.text: The change arrived by task. Calculation moved first; capture and editing of map features followed later. Chapter 3 picks up that second step.
